To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

local mRNA delivery of IL-36γ and IL-23 cytokines and the T cell costimulatory molecule OX40L to solid tumors can lead to durable and systemic antitumor immunity, which can be enhanced by checkpoint blockade in tumors resistant to this treatment.
direct intratumoral administration (IT) of mRNAs for the inflammatory cytokine IL-36γ and the T cell costimulators OX40L and IL-23 induces robust anticancer responses and systemic immunity.

intratumoral mRNA delivery of a combination of cytokine and OX40 ligand mRNAs can produce potent anticancer effects across multiple tumor models and that the combination can be used to render tumors resistant to immune checkpoint blockade.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new therapeutic approach for cancer treatment based on the use of mRNA as a vehicle to express cytokines and co-stimulatory molecules in the tumor microenvironment.
developing mRNA-based immunotherapy that can overcome tumor immunosuppression, leading to durable responses across multiple tumor models.
the use of mRNA to induce a potent antitumor immune response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the combination of IL-23/36γ/OX4L triplet mRNA mixture induced potent and durable antitumor immunity in multiple tumor models.
local mRNA therapy encoding inflammatory factors and T cell costimulators mediates persistent anticumor immunity.
the combination of IL-23/ IL-36γ/Ox40L mRNA treatment is a novel and effective approach to cancer immunotherapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
local delivery of mRNA encoding IL-36γ and IL-23 in conjunction with OX40L can generate a durable antitumor immunity in a variety of tumor types.

local mRNA therapy encoding inflammatory IL-23, OX40L and IL-36γ mRNAs mediates potent, durable, and cross-tumor type anticancer immunity, and can synergize with checkpoint blockade to overcome tumor resistance to immune therapy.
we found a way to use mRNAs to induce a robust and persistent immune response against cancer, even in immunologically “cold” tumors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
intratumoral administration with mRNA encoding cytokines can lead to robust antitumor immunity in a variety of models.
local mRNA therapy encoding inflammatory factors and a T cell costimulator can induce potent and durable antitumor immunity in diverse models.
intratumoral delivery can induce durable antitumor immunity, even in tumors with low levels of immune cell infiltration and with poor responses to checkpoint blockade.
